newsitem.title: USA: Record imports limit improvement in U.S. trade gap.
newsitem.headline: Record imports limit improvement in U.S. trade gap.

text.p: A booming U.S. economy drew in record imports during February, the Commerce Department said on Thursday, slowing improvement in the monthly deficit and spotlighting trade tensions with China.

The gap between imports and exports fell 8.5 percent to $11.59 billion. But analysts said that still was "atrociously high" and would be hard to reduce while a soaring dollar makes popular Japanese cars and other imported goods cheaper for eager American consumers.

Overall imports were up 2.1 percent in February to $85.05 billion. Imports of foreign-made industrial supplies and materials used by U.S. manufacturers, capital goods and cars, parts and engines all hit record levels.
Exports also rose by 4 percent from January to a record $73.46 billion, helped by a bulge in commercial aircraft sales to Britain and by a modest fall in costs for imported oil and other energy.
Economists said that a rising dollar and higher imports helped keep U.S. consumer prices in check but also set the stage for long-term problems.

"Right now, we need this to let some steam out of an overheating economy," said economist Sung Won Sohn of Norwest Corp. in Minneapolis. "But long term, it's quite worrisome because these deficits are actually rising on a trend basis."

Phildaelphia-based economist Joel Naroff of First Union Corp. noted the deficit in the first two months of 1997 exceeded the comparable 1996 two-month total by 46 percent. He called February's deficit "simply atrocious."

Razor and cosmetics maker Gillette Co., at its annual meeting in Boston, directly blamed the dollar for shaving its worldwide sales by three percentage points in the first three months this year. Carmakers and computer companies like International Business Machines Corp. also have complained that the strong dollar hurts their business.

Separately on Thursday, the Labour Department said new applications for jobless benefits picked up last week to 332,000 from 324,000 in the previous week -- possibly also a helpful development in the short run.
"The data suggest that the momentum in the labour force may be leveling out," said William Sullivan, senior vice-president of Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. in New York.

The Federal Reserve, which raised short-term interest rates a quarter percentage point late last month, has cited its concern that tight labour markets risk ingniting inflationary wage demands and price rises.
Fed Vice-Chairwoman Alice Rivlin, speaking to a business group Thursday, said she saw no sign the economy was "running out of steam or generating any obvious imbalances."
She said central bank policy-makers were exercising "prudence and a bit of insurance" when they raised rates to sustain the long-running expansion, now in its seventh year.

A report from the Federal Reserve bank of Philadelphia said its index of manufacturing activity dropped sharply to 5.7 in April from 21.1 in March as new orders waned and hiring weakened, while prices for goods accelerated.
Economist Michael Trebing of the Philadelphia Fed said there clearly was "some slowing in the growth rate" regionally but cautioned that it might not mean a national slowdown is at hand.

The trade report showed a strong improvement in business with Western Europe, where the United States posted a surplus of $291 million in February -- a sharp reversal from January's $1.34 billion deficit.
Most of that was because exports of commercial aircraft quadrupled to more than $1 billion in February from $263 million in January.
The trade picture with Asia remained muddied.

The politically sensitive deficit with Japan -- the biggest with any single country -- was down 0.9 percent to $4.26 billion. The shortfall with China narrowed 9.6 percent from January to $3.37 billion but exports to China actually were lower in February.

"We're now facing a double-whammy. Every single month Japan and China are giving us a one-two punch and in the future it's going to be China that is leading the assault," said Sohn. He noted China was primarily buying high-tech machinery from the United States with the intent fo further boost its manufactured exports.
Commerce Secretary William Daley said China was a worry.

"China remains the only major market in the world where U.S. exports are not growing," Daley told a news conference. "This export picture remains an object of concern to me and to the administration.'

Record exports to Canada helped lower the bilateral deficit with that country by 12.9 percent in February to $1.48 billion. The shortfall with oil-producing OPEC countries, which had ballooned earlier in the winter, declined 4.2 percent to $2.55 billion.
During February, exports of American-made capital goods jumped by $1.32 billion to $22.7 billion while overseas sales of commercial aircraft rose $625 million to $1.72 billion.
